lesson.title: Circles That Show Overlap: Mapping Events Visually
lesson.summary: A Venn diagram draws the sample space as a rectangle and each event as a circle inside it, so intersections, unions, and complements are all visible as regions rather than formulas.
lesson.body:
Recall that an event is just a subset of the outcomes in a sample space, the outcomes you have decided to pay attention to, and that the complement of an event is everything in the sample space that is not in it. A Venn diagram gives both ideas a physical shape. Draw a rectangle to represent the entire sample space, every possible outcome. Inside it, draw a circle for each event you care about. Any point inside a circle belongs to that event; any point outside all the circles belongs to the complement of everything drawn, meaning none of the events happened.

When you draw two circles that overlap, the diagram is showing you, at a glance, four distinct regions: the part of the first circle that does not touch the second (only the first event happened), the part of the second circle that does not touch the first (only the second event happened), the lens shaped overlap where both circles cover the same point (both events happened, the intersection, the word "and"), and the space outside both circles but still inside the rectangle (neither event happened, the complement of their union).

Here is a worked example. Among 50 students, 20 take Spanish and 15 take French, and 8 take both. Draw two overlapping circles inside a rectangle labeled with all 50 students. Put 8 in the lens shaped overlap, since that is the count of students in both languages. The Spanish circle needs to total 20 students, and 8 of those are already in the overlap, so the Spanish only region holds 20 minus 8, which is 12 students. Similarly, the French circle needs to total 15, and 8 are already in the overlap, so the French only region holds 15 minus 8, which is 7 students.

Now find the region outside both circles, the students taking neither language, using the complement idea directly: add up everyone accounted for inside the circles, 12 plus 7 plus 8, which is 27 students taking at least one language. Since the rectangle holds all 50 students, the complement of that union is 50 minus 27, which is 23 students taking neither Spanish nor French. As a check, all four regions should add back up to the whole class: 12 plus 7 plus 8 plus 23 equals 50, which they do.

This picture is doing double duty. The overlap region is literally the intersection you will use for the general addition rule next, and the outside region is literally the complement of event idea applied to two events at once instead of one, everything left over once you remove both circles from the rectangle.
